Q.situation_summary: Cristina reports mold in her 3-room flat in Zurich, first noticed last month on the bedroom wall behind the bed and now also near the window, describing a bad smell. She says she informed the landlord’s property manager by phone, who attributed the mold to insufficient ventilation and advised wiping it with vinegar. Cristina states she opens windows every morning and has taken photos. She is considering paying 30% less rent this month or moving out, and asks about her rights and next steps.
legal_statements: The landlord must keep the flat fit for the agreed use. If a defect appears that the tenant did not cause and does not have to fix at their own cost, the tenant can demand that the landlord repairs it, and can also claim a proportionate rent reduction and damages. The tenant only has to fix small things at their own cost (minor cleaning or small repairs that are part of normal upkeep, according to local custom). Lease clauses that weaken the landlord's duty to keep a flat fit for use, to the tenant's disadvantage, are void. If the landlord says the tenant caused the defect (for example mould from too little airing), that is a disputed fact: it is not decided here, and evidence on both sides matters.  [OR Art. 256 Abs. 1, OR Art. 256 Abs. 2, OR Art. 259, OR Art. 259a Abs. 1]

If the defect reduces the use of the flat, the tenant can ask the landlord for a rent reduction that matches the impairment. It runs from the day the landlord learned of the defect until the defect is fixed. A phone call can count, but a letter or e-mail is easier to prove. If the defect has caused the tenant damage (for example damaged belongings or extra costs), the landlord must pay for it unless the landlord proves it was not their fault. The tenant must report defects that they do not have to fix themselves; if they do not, they can be liable for the resulting damage.  [OR Art. 259a Abs. 1, OR Art. 259d, OR Art. 259e, OR Art. 257g Abs. 1, OR Art. 257g Abs. 2]

Warning: the tenant should not simply pay less rent, or stop paying, because of a defect. The law does not provide for the tenant to cut or hold back rent on their own. If rent is not paid in full, the landlord can treat the missing amount as arrears: set a written payment deadline (at least 30 days for a flat) and, if it is not paid in time, terminate the lease with at least 30 days' notice to the end of a month. Whether a reduction is justified, and by how much, is settled by agreement with the landlord or, failing that, through the conciliation authority (Schlichtungsbehörde, the local tenancy dispute office) and, if needed, a court. The lawful alternative to paying the landlord is the deposit procedure.  [OR Art. 257d Abs. 1, OR Art. 257d Abs. 2, OR Art. 259d, OR Art. 259g Abs. 1]

Rent deposit (Hinterlegung), the legal way to put pressure on the landlord: (1) the tenant asks the landlord in writing to fix the defect within a reasonable deadline and, to be able to deposit rent, warns in the same letter that, if it is not fixed in time, future rent will be paid to the office designated by the canton; (2) if the deadline passes, the tenant announces the deposit to the landlord in writing; (3) rent that falls due after that is paid to the designated office instead of the landlord, and counts as paid. (4) Within 30 days of the due date of the first deposited rent, the tenant must bring their claims (for example repair, rent reduction) to the conciliation authority; otherwise the deposited rent goes to the landlord. The landlord can also ask the conciliation authority to release rent that was deposited wrongly. Only rent that falls due in the future can be deposited. Every step must be followed exactly, so get advice before starting.  [OR Art. 259a Abs. 2, OR Art. 259g Abs. 1, OR Art. 259g Abs. 2, OR Art. 259h Abs. 1, OR Art. 259h Abs. 2]

If the landlord knows about a defect and does not fix it within a reasonable time: (a) if the defect makes the flat unfit for its use or seriously impairs its use, the tenant may terminate the lease without notice; (b) if the defect reduces the use but does not seriously impair it, the tenant may have it repaired at the landlord's cost. Whether a defect is serious enough, and what time is reasonable, depends on the case. Setting a clear written repair deadline first makes the situation easier to prove. A tenant's termination must be in writing and signed; if the flat is the family home of a married couple or registered partners, the other spouse or partner must expressly agree. Get advice before terminating or ordering repairs, because these steps can be costly if the conditions are not met.  [OR Art. 259b, OR Art. 266l Abs. 1, OR Art. 266m Abs. 1, OR Art. 266m Abs. 3]
actions: Advise the client to keep paying the full rent on time until there is an agreement on a reduction or the deposit procedure has been started correctly. If rent has already been held back, or a payment demand has arrived, get advice from the tenant association at once: a payment demand has a strict deadline.

Refer the client to the tenant association (Mieterinnen- und Mieterverband) or the conciliation authority for advice before depositing rent, terminating the lease or ordering repairs. Conciliation authorities must also advise tenants outside a procedure.

Help the client send the landlord a dated letter (ideally registered) or e-mail: describe the defect and when it started, say when the landlord was first told (including phone calls), ask for repair by a reasonable deadline, and state that a rent reduction is claimed from the date the landlord learned of the defect. If the client may want to deposit rent later, the letter must also warn that future rent will be deposited if the deadline passes. Keep a copy.

Ask the client to keep evidence: dated photos and videos, a log of every contact with the landlord (date, person, what was said), notes on the extent of the problem over time (for example room temperatures, size of mould patches), and receipts for any extra costs. Where the landlord blames the tenant, also note airing and heating habits.

legal_statements: A payment demand is not yet a termination. It is the first of two steps: the landlord sets a written payment deadline, which for a flat must be at least 30 days, and warns that the lease will be terminated if the deadline passes without payment. Only if the deadline passes without payment may the landlord take the second step: a separate termination on the official cantonal form, with at least 30 days' notice to the end of a month. The lease does not end by itself when the deadline passes, and a flat cannot be terminated with immediate effect for arrears.  [OR Art. 257d Abs. 1, OR Art. 257d Abs. 2, OR Art. 266l Abs. 2]

If the full amount owed is paid within the deadline, the landlord cannot terminate the lease on the basis of this payment demand. A part payment may not be enough. The law makes no exception for hardship such as job loss, children or a pending application for social assistance, so more time is only possible if the landlord agrees to it. Whether such a termination can be challenged is a separate question; a challenge must be filed with the conciliation authority (Schlichtungsbehörde) within 30 days of receiving the termination.  [OR Art. 272a Abs. 1, OR Art. 273 Abs. 1]

For notice of a rent increase or other unilateral contract change, a mechanically reproduced signature on the prescribed form is sufficient. Art. 270b OR: The tenant may challenge a rent increase as abusive under Articles 269 and 269a at the conciliation authority within 30 days of receiving notice of the increase. rules: Art. 269 OR: Rent is abusive if it yields an excessive return from the rental property or if it is based on an obviously excessive purchase price.

The tenant must submit a written request for rent reduction to the landlord, who must respond within 30 days. If the landlord does not grant the request, only grants it partially, or fails to respond within the 30-day period, the tenant may refer the matter to the conciliation authority within 30 days. If the tenant files a request for rent reduction at the same time as challenging a rent increase, paragraph 2 does not apply.

Art. 270b OR: The tenant may challenge a rent increase as abusive under Articles 269 and 269a at the conciliation authority within 30 days of receiving notice of the increase. If the landlord unilaterally changes the rental contract to the tenant's disadvantage—such as reducing previous services or introducing new ancillary costs—paragraph 1 applies.

Maria and her family are concerned they cannot afford the higher rent and fear losing their apartment.
legal_statements: A rent increase must be sent on a form approved by the canton and must give reasons. The increase is void if it is not on that form, if it gives no reasons, or if the landlord threatens or gives a termination together with it. The form must show the old and new rent and ancillary costs, the date from which the increase applies, a clear reason (with a separate amount for each reason if there are several), and how to challenge it. If the reasons are in a covering letter, the form must say so. A printed signature is enough. The same rules apply to other one-sided changes at the tenant's expense, such as new ancillary costs or reduced services. Exception: for rent steps fixed in the lease, a written notice is enough.  [OR Art. 269d Abs. 1, OR Art. 269d Abs. 2, OR Art. 269d Abs. 3, OR Art. 269d Abs. 4, OR Art. 269d Abs. 5, VMWG Art. 19 Abs. 1, VMWG Art. 19 Abs. 1bis]

The landlord can raise the rent only to the next date on which the lease could be terminated (under the notice period and termination dates that apply to the lease). The notice must reach the tenant at least 10 days before that notice period begins. If it arrived later, the increase cannot take effect on the date stated; the tenant association can say from when it could apply.  [OR Art. 269d Abs. 1, OR Art. 266a Abs. 1, OR Art. 266c]

The tenant can challenge the increase as abusive at the conciliation authority (Schlichtungsbehörde, the local tenancy dispute office) within 30 days after it was communicated. The 30 days count from receipt, not from the date the new rent starts. Asking the landlord to explain the figures does not stop the 30 days. Once the 30 days have passed, the increase can no longer be challenged as abusive (whether it is void for a form defect is a separate question). Valid rent steps fixed in advance in the lease cannot be challenged in this way. The conciliation procedure in disputes about flats has no court costs.  [OR Art. 270b Abs. 1, OR Art. 270b Abs. 2, OR Art. 270d, VMWG Art. 20 Abs. 1, ZPO Art. 113 Abs. 2]

In general terms, a rent is abusive if it gives the landlord an excessive return from the flat or is based on a clearly excessive purchase price. A rent is usually not abusive if, for example, it is within the usual rents for the area, is justified by higher costs or extra services or improvements from the landlord, or only offsets inflation on the landlord's risk capital. Whether a given increase is justified depends on the figures. In the conciliation procedure the tenant can ask for the supporting documents for every reason given.  [OR Art. 269, OR Art. 269a, VMWG Art. 20 Abs. 2]

If the increase is challenged and no agreement is reached at the conciliation authority, the existing lease continues unchanged during the conciliation procedure (and during a court procedure, subject to interim orders of the court). A termination given because the landlord wants to push through a rent increase, or given during a conciliation or court procedure about the tenancy, can be challenged; the protection during a procedure has exceptions, for example a termination for rent arrears.  [OR Art. 270e, OR Art. 271a Abs. 1, OR Art. 271a Abs. 3]

A written request naming the landlord, stating that the increase is challenged, and enclosing a copy of the notice is enough to start; it can also be made orally at the authority. Do not wait for the landlord's answer or for full documents.

They have contacted the property management twice and a technician visited once, but the issue remains unresolved. The property management attributes the problem to supply issues with a spare part. The family feels helpless and the youngest child has developed a cold. They are asking whether they are permitted to pay reduced rent.
legal_statements: The landlord must keep the flat fit for the agreed use. If a defect appears that the tenant did not cause and does not have to fix at their own cost, the tenant can demand that the landlord repairs it, and can also claim a proportionate rent reduction and damages. The tenant only has to fix small things at their own cost (minor cleaning or small repairs that are part of normal upkeep, according to local custom). Lease clauses that weaken the landlord's duty to keep a flat fit for use, to the tenant's disadvantage, are void. If the landlord says the tenant caused the defect (for example mould from too little airing), that is a disputed fact: it is not decided here, and evidence on both sides matters.  [OR Art. 256 Abs. 1, OR Art. 256 Abs. 2, OR Art. 259, OR Art. 259a Abs. 1]

If the defect reduces the use of the flat, the tenant can ask the landlord for a rent reduction that matches the impairment. It runs from the day the landlord learned of the defect until the defect is fixed. A phone call can count, but a letter or e-mail is easier to prove. If the defect has caused the tenant damage (for example damaged belongings or extra costs), the landlord must pay for it unless the landlord proves it was not their fault. The tenant must report defects that they do not have to fix themselves; if they do not, they can be liable for the resulting damage.  [OR Art. 259a Abs. 1, OR Art. 259d, OR Art. 259e, OR Art. 257g Abs. 1, OR Art. 257g Abs. 2]

Warning: the tenant should not simply pay less rent, or stop paying, because of a defect. The law does not provide for the tenant to cut or hold back rent on their own. If rent is not paid in full, the landlord can treat the missing amount as arrears: set a written payment deadline (at least 30 days for a flat) and, if it is not paid in time, terminate the lease with at least 30 days' notice to the end of a month. Whether a reduction is justified, and by how much, is settled by agreement with the landlord or, failing that, through the conciliation authority (Schlichtungsbehörde, the local tenancy dispute office) and, if needed, a court. The lawful alternative to paying the landlord is the deposit procedure.  [OR Art. 257d Abs. 1, OR Art. 257d Abs. 2, OR Art. 259d, OR Art. 259g Abs. 1]

Rent deposit (Hinterlegung), the legal way to put pressure on the landlord: (1) the tenant asks the landlord in writing to fix the defect within a reasonable deadline and, to be able to deposit rent, warns in the same letter that, if it is not fixed in time, future rent will be paid to the office designated by the canton; (2) if the deadline passes, the tenant announces the deposit to the landlord in writing; (3) rent that falls due after that is paid to the designated office instead of the landlord, and counts as paid. (4) Within 30 days of the due date of the first deposited rent, the tenant must bring their claims (for example repair, rent reduction) to the conciliation authority; otherwise the deposited rent goes to the landlord. The landlord can also ask the conciliation authority to release rent that was deposited wrongly. Only rent that falls due in the future can be deposited. Every step must be followed exactly, so get advice before starting.  [OR Art. 259a Abs. 2, OR Art. 259g Abs. 1, OR Art. 259g Abs. 2, OR Art. 259h Abs. 1, OR Art. 259h Abs. 2]

If the landlord knows about a defect and does not fix it within a reasonable time: (a) if the defect makes the flat unfit for its use or seriously impairs its use, the tenant may terminate the lease without notice; (b) if the defect reduces the use but does not seriously impair it, the tenant may have it repaired at the landlord's cost. Whether a defect is serious enough, and what time is reasonable, depends on the case. Setting a clear written repair deadline first makes the situation easier to prove. A tenant's termination must be in writing and signed; if the flat is the family home of a married couple or registered partners, the other spouse or partner must expressly agree. Get advice before terminating or ordering repairs, because these steps can be costly if the conditions are not met.  [OR Art. 259b, OR Art. 266l Abs. 1, OR Art. 266m Abs. 1, OR Art. 266m Abs. 3]

Contact the landlord or property management today (and the building's emergency number or caretaker if they cannot be reached). Ask in writing for an immediate interim solution (for example temporary heaters) and a date for the full repair. If nothing happens quickly, contact the tenant association or the conciliation authority the same week.

legal_statements: A landlord must terminate a flat lease in writing, on a form approved by the canton that explains how to challenge the termination or ask for an extension. A termination without this form is void (has no legal effect).  [OR Art. 266l Abs. 1, OR Art. 266l Abs. 2, OR Art. 266o]

A termination can be challenged at the conciliation authority (Schlichtungsbehörde) within 30 days of receipt. The 30 days run from receipt, not from the end date of the lease. A challenge is possible even if the termination gives no reason. A termination is challengeable if it breaks the principle of good faith; the law names examples, such as a termination given because the tenant asserted claims under the lease in good faith (for example, asking for a defect to be repaired). Such a termination is not automatically void: it must be challenged in time, and the outcome is not certain. Conciliation proceedings in disputes about flat leases are free of court fees.  [OR Art. 271 Abs. 1, OR Art. 271a Abs. 1, OR Art. 259a Abs. 1, OR Art. 273 Abs. 1, ZPO Art. 113 Abs. 2]
The landlord must give the reasons for the termination if the tenant asks. Asking for the reasons does not change the 30-day deadline for a challenge.  [OR Art. 271 Abs. 2, OR Art. 273 Abs. 1]

If the end of the lease would cause the tenant or the family a hardship that the landlord's interests do not justify, the tenant can ask for an extension of the tenancy (Erstreckung: extra time before having to leave). For a flat, the authority can grant up to four years in total, in one or two steps. For an open-ended lease, the request must be filed with the conciliation authority within 30 days of receipt of the termination. If a challenge is rejected, the authority checks on its own whether an extension can be granted. An extension is excluded after some terminations, for example for unpaid rent after a payment demand, for a serious breach of the duty of care and consideration, or for the tenant's bankruptcy; it is usually excluded if the landlord offers an equivalent replacement flat.  [OR Art. 272 Abs. 1, OR Art. 272a Abs. 1, OR Art. 272a Abs. 2, OR Art. 272b Abs. 1, OR Art. 273 Abs. 2, OR Art. 273 Abs. 5]

The landlord must keep the flat fit for the agreed use. If a defect appears that the tenant did not cause and does not have to fix at their own cost, the tenant can demand that the landlord repairs it, and can also claim a proportionate rent reduction and damages. The tenant only has to fix small things at their own cost (minor cleaning or small repairs that are part of normal upkeep, according to local custom). Lease clauses that weaken the landlord's duty to keep a flat fit for use, to the tenant's disadvantage, are void. If the landlord says the tenant caused the defect (for example mould from too little airing), that is a disputed fact: it is not decided here, and evidence on both sides matters.  [OR Art. 256 Abs. 1, OR Art. 256 Abs. 2, OR Art. 259, OR Art. 259a Abs. 1]

If the defect reduces the use of the flat, the tenant can ask the landlord for a rent reduction that matches the impairment. It runs from the day the landlord learned of the defect until the defect is fixed. A phone call can count, but a letter or e-mail is easier to prove. If the defect has caused the tenant damage (for example damaged belongings or extra costs), the landlord must pay for it unless the landlord proves it was not their fault. The tenant must report defects that they do not have to fix themselves; if they do not, they can be liable for the resulting damage.  [OR Art. 259a Abs. 1, OR Art. 259d, OR Art. 259e, OR Art. 257g Abs. 1, OR Art. 257g Abs. 2]

Warning: the tenant should not simply pay less rent, or stop paying, because of a defect. The law does not provide for the tenant to cut or hold back rent on their own. If rent is not paid in full, the landlord can treat the missing amount as arrears: set a written payment deadline (at least 30 days for a flat) and, if it is not paid in time, terminate the lease with at least 30 days' notice to the end of a month. Whether a reduction is justified, and by how much, is settled by agreement with the landlord or, failing that, through the conciliation authority (Schlichtungsbehörde, the local tenancy dispute office) and, if needed, a court. The lawful alternative to paying the landlord is the deposit procedure.  [OR Art. 257d Abs. 1, OR Art. 257d Abs. 2, OR Art. 259d, OR Art. 259g Abs. 1]

Rent deposit (Hinterlegung), the legal way to put pressure on the landlord: (1) the tenant asks the landlord in writing to fix the defect within a reasonable deadline and, to be able to deposit rent, warns in the same letter that, if it is not fixed in time, future rent will be paid to the office designated by the canton; (2) if the deadline passes, the tenant announces the deposit to the landlord in writing; (3) rent that falls due after that is paid to the designated office instead of the landlord, and counts as paid. (4) Within 30 days of the due date of the first deposited rent, the tenant must bring their claims (for example repair, rent reduction) to the conciliation authority; otherwise the deposited rent goes to the landlord. The landlord can also ask the conciliation authority to release rent that was deposited wrongly. Only rent that falls due in the future can be deposited. Every step must be followed exactly, so get advice before starting.  [OR Art. 259a Abs. 2, OR Art. 259g Abs. 1, OR Art. 259g Abs. 2, OR Art. 259h Abs. 1, OR Art. 259h Abs. 2]

If the landlord knows about a defect and does not fix it within a reasonable time: (a) if the defect makes the flat unfit for its use or seriously impairs its use, the tenant may terminate the lease without notice; (b) if the defect reduces the use but does not seriously impair it, the tenant may have it repaired at the landlord's cost. Whether a defect is serious enough, and what time is reasonable, depends on the case. Setting a clear written repair deadline first makes the situation easier to prove. A tenant's termination must be in writing and signed; if the flat is the family home of a married couple or registered partners, the other spouse or partner must expressly agree. Get advice before terminating or ordering repairs, because these steps can be costly if the conditions are not met.  [OR Art. 259b, OR Art. 266l Abs. 1, OR Art. 266m Abs. 1, OR Art. 266m Abs. 3]

If the landlord has given notice after the tenant reported a defect or asked for a repair: a termination given because the tenant asserts claims from the lease in good faith can be challenged. A challenge must be submitted to the conciliation authority within 30 days of receiving the termination. A challenge is not automatically successful; it depends on the facts.  [OR Art. 271a Abs. 1, OR Art. 273 Abs. 1]

legal_statements: Usually, if both signed the lease, each co-tenant owes the landlord the whole rent, not just a share (joint and several liability, 'solidarisch'). Leases often say this expressly, so check the lease for such a clause; the law also provides it for people who jointly took on an obligation as a simple partnership, unless they agreed otherwise. Where this applies, the landlord can claim the whole rent or part of it from either co-tenant, and both stay bound until the whole amount is paid. One co-tenant moving out does not change this by itself.  [OR Art. 143 Abs. 1, OR Art. 143 Abs. 2, OR Art. 544 Abs. 3, OR Art. 144 Abs. 1, OR Art. 144 Abs. 2]

Where the co-tenants are jointly liable, a co-tenant who pays more than his or her share can usually claim the excess back from the other. Unless something else follows from their relationship, each bears an equal share.  [OR Art. 148 Abs. 1, OR Art. 148 Abs. 2]

If only part of the rent arrives, the rest is in arrears. The landlord can then set a written payment deadline of at least 30 days and warn that the lease will be terminated. If the arrears are not paid within that deadline, the landlord can terminate with at least 30 days' notice to the end of a month. After such a termination, an extension of the tenancy is not possible.  [OR Art. 257d Abs. 1, OR Art. 257d Abs. 2, OR Art. 272a Abs. 1]

A tenant's notice must be in writing. A notice given by only one co-tenant may not end the lease for everyone. Whether it has any effect, for that person or for both, is not settled by the law text and is a question for a tenancy professional. Until that is clear, do not assume the lease has ended, and keep the full rent paid where possible.  [OR Art. 266l Abs. 1, OR Art. 257d Abs. 1]

The bank may pay it out only with the agreement of both the landlord and the tenant side, or on a final payment order or court judgment, so one co-tenant moving out does not by itself release the deposit or a share of it. They do not apply to unmarried partners, even with a child together. Under tenancy law, an unmarried partner's position comes from being a tenant herself or himself, if she or he signed the lease.
